domain_restrictions: m is an integer and m is at least 1.
t has exactly m minus 1 entries.
Each entry t sub i is either plus one or minus one.
When m equals 1, the sequence t is empty.
The definition of Peak of t for the nontrivial case only applies when m is at least 2.
The index j in the peak membership rule ranges over integers between 2 and m minus 1.
The index i in the final sign pattern characterizations ranges over integers between 1 and m minus 1.
semantic_sketch_json.normalized_claim: For every positive integer m and every sign sequence t of length m minus 1, the set Peak of t defined by the endpoint and adjacent sign rules has no consecutive integers. When m is at least 2, Peak of t is the set of odd positions in 1 through m exactly when the signs alternate minus one, plus one, minus one, and so on starting with minus one, and Peak of t is the set of even positions in 1 through m exactly when the signs alternate plus one, minus one, plus one, and so on starting with plus one.
quantifier_order: For every integer m with m at least 1.
For every sign sequence t of length m minus 1, with each entry equal to plus one or minus one.
Define Peak of t by cases depending on whether m equals 1 or m is at least 2.

If m is at least 2, for each integer j with 2 at most j at most m minus 1, membership of j in Peak of t is determined by the adjacent signs t sub j minus 1 and t sub j, with the endpoints handled separately.
If m is at least 2, for every index i from 1 to m minus 1, the odd peak characterization uses the condition t sub i equals minus one to the i.
If m is at least 2, for every index i from 1 to m minus 1, the even peak characterization uses the condition t sub i equals minus one to the i minus 1.

The parity characterizations depend on the entire family of equalities for all indices i from 1 to m minus 1.
The set Peak of t is determined uniquely by m and t once the sign sequence is fixed.

statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 1, and let t = (t_1,...,t_{m-1}) be a sign sequence with each t_i in {+1,-1}; when m = 1 this sequence is empty. Define Peak(t) subseteq {1,...,m} by: if m = 1 then Peak(t) = {1}; if m >= 2 then 1 belongs to Peak(t) exactly when t_1 = -1, m belongs to Peak(t) exactly when t_{m-1} = +1, and for each integer j with 2 <= j <= m-1, j belongs to Peak(t) exactly when t_{j-1} = +1 and t_j = -1. Then Peak(t) contains no two consecutive integers. If m >= 2, then Peak(t) is exactly the set of odd integers in {1,...,m} if and only if t_i = (-1)^i for every i, and Peak(t) is exactly the set of even integers in {1,...,m} if and only if t_i = (-1)^(i-1) for every i.
